name: Brimonidine gel (Mirvaso)

card.summary: A prescription vasoconstrictor gel approved in 2013 for facial redness in rosacea; it works within hours but is temporary, and rebound redness has been reported.
card.note: Case reports describe rebound or paradoxical redness, allergic contact dermatitis and, rarely, bradycardia.

quick.overview:
Mirvaso is a 0.33% brimonidine tartrate gel that the FDA approved in 2013 for the facial redness of rosacea. Brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist also used in eye drops for glaucoma and for eye redness.

It is discussed as a temporary redness reducer that narrows skin blood vessels, with an effect that peaks within hours of application. Published case reports also describe rebound or worsened redness in some users.
quick.mechanism: Brimonidine activates alpha-2 adrenergic receptors in the skin's blood vessels, causing them to constrict and reducing visible redness. Rosacea overviews place this effect at roughly 3 to 6 hours after application.
quick.risks: Reported adverse effects include flushing or redness worse than baseline, allergic contact dermatitis, severe rebound erythema in case reports, and one reported case of symptomatic bradycardia. It is prescription-only in many countries.

lead: Brimonidine gel (Mirvaso, brimonidine tartrate 0.33%) was approved by the US FDA in 2013 for facial erythema of rosacea and was described at launch as the first drug aimed at the hallmark redness of the condition [3]. Brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, first patented in 1972 and in medical use since 1996 for eye conditions [7].

Rosacea overviews describe brimonidine as constricting vessels to reduce redness, with a peak effect 3 to 6 hours after application [7]. A review of facial erythema in rosacea places the redness in the context of immune dysregulation and neurovascular dysfunction [1].
Published case reports describe adverse reactions including allergic contact dermatitis [2][5], rebound erythema [6][3] and a case of symptomatic bradycardia [8].

paras: The gel is indicated for persistent facial redness of rosacea in adults [3][7]. The same ingredient appears in ophthalmic products for glaucoma and ocular redness, some available over the counter in the US [7].

A 2014 Drug and Therapeutics Bulletin appraisal and a SkinMed product summary reviewed the product at launch [9][10]. A small imaging study used optical coherence tomography to monitor treatment response [4]. Registered post-marketing studies include open-label studies of 101 and 205 participants and a 301-person utilisation and satisfaction survey [11][12][13]; results are not summarised here. Because the effect is a vessel constriction, rosacea references describe it as reducing redness during the hours of effect rather than altering the disease [7].

Commonly reported adverse events include redness or flushing worse than baseline, most often with the first application [3]. Case reports describe a paradoxical erythema reaction with long-term use [3], severe rebound erythema labelled dermatitis medicamentosa [6], and allergic contact dermatitis, including sensitisation in two cases [2][5]. A 2024 case report described symptomatic bradycardia after use [8]. Systemic effects of brimonidine in other forms include low blood pressure and dry mouth [7].
Brimonidine constricts blood vessels through alpha-2 adrenergic activation, which in the skin reduces redness [7].

Human studies include open-label post-marketing trials in rosacea [11][12], a utilisation study [13] and a small imaging study [4]. Studies in other conditions (hand-foot syndrome, flushing in aldehyde dehydrogenase deficiency) are registered but concern other uses [14][15].
The gel is mentioned in skincare circles as an option for temporary redness before events, typically alongside discussion of rebound redness reports.

timeline.event: FDA approves Mirvaso gel 0.33% for facial erythema of rosacea. [3]
